entries.title: Netanyahu rejects Trump-backed Gaza peace plan
entries.summary: The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.
entries.content:
Middle East

Netanyahu rejects Trump-backed Gaza peace plan

August 10, 2026

The Israeli prime minister says his country will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms, putting him at odds with a US-backed roadmap endorsed by the group.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."

Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."

The White House did not immediately comment.

What does Trump's Gaza plan say about Hamas disarmament?

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.

The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.

Gaza plan rejected by Netanyahu 'only way forward':

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.

However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.

"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."

How are Israel's elections affecting Netanyahu's Gaza policy?

The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.

"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."

The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.

The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.

Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.

Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Alleged Irish crime boss Kinahan charged with directing criminal organisation
entries.summary: Daniel Kinahan is accused of leading the Kinahan organised crime group, an international network linked to drug trafficking and money laundering operations,
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

Daniel Kinahan is accused of leading the Kinahan organised crime group, an international network linked to drug trafficking and money laundering operations,

Suspected international crime boss Daniel Kinahan landed in Ireland on Sunday after being extradited from the United Arab Emirates.

Following his arrival in Ireland, prosecutors charged Kinahan with directing a criminal organization during a special court sitting.

Kinahan, 49, was arrested in April in Dubai after Ireland issued a warrant for "alleged serious organized crime offenses."

He is accused of being the leader of a cartel linked to drug smuggling and money laundering.

What do we know about the allegations against Kinahan?

The group is thought to be the most powerful criminal organization in Ireland, with Irish police estimating its wealth at more than €1 billion ($1.15 billion).

The alleged crime boss had lived openly in the UAE for about a decade before his arrest. He moved there from Spain around 2016 after the murder of one of his associates and an attempt on his life.

In 2022, the United States imposed sanctions on Kinahan after linking his organization to some of the world's most notorious crime networks and offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The group is linked to a brutal feud with a smaller Irish syndicate that has resulted in 18 murders.

“Since February 2016, the (Kinahan Organized Crime Group) has been involved in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, resulting in numerous murders, including of two innocent bystanders,” the US Treasury Department said.

Kinahan is the second alleged senior member of the cartel to be extradited to Ireland from Dubai. Sean McGovern was extradited in 2024 and was ultimately sentenced to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organized crime and attempted murder.

Irish media reported that a special security convoy would be deployed to escort Kinahan to the Special Criminal Court, which handles offenses related to terrorism and organized crime.

UAE, Ireland hail judicial cooperation in Kinahan extradition

In a joint statement, the justice minister of the UAE and Ireland called Kinahan "one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organized crime."

Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan called the extradition a "landmark of judicial cooperation with Dubai," adding that it "sends a clear message that suspected perpetrators of serious and organized crime will find no safe haven from justice."

Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Helen McEntee hailed the outcome as "the culmination of years of determined work" by Irish authorities under various governments.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Syria says deal agreed with Russia on future of military bases
entries.summary: Under the agreement, Syria will take over management of two Russian bases that were used to support ousted leader Bashar Assad during the Syrian civil war.
entries.content:
Syria

Syria says deal agreed on future of Russian bases

August 9, 2026

Under the agreement, Syria will take over management of two Russian bases that were used to support ousted leader Bashar Assad during the Syrian civil war.

Syria and Russia have agreed on the future management of Russian bases on the country's Mediterranean coast.

Russia used the bases to provide military support to former Syrian leader Bashar Assad during Syria's 13-year civil war that ended in 2024.

The Syrian Foreign Ministry announced Sunday that the two nations had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) after 18 months of negotiations.

The deal effectively means Russia will no longer have military outposts in the Arab country.

What will happen to Russia's military bases in Syria?

Syria will take over management of the Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, Syria's Foreign Ministry said.

State media cited the ministry as saying that the bases would be converted into "joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests."

The facilities will be gradually integrated into the country's civilian administration. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, the ministry said.

Russia has yet to comment on the agreement.

Russia trying to build relations with post-Assad Syria

During the civil war in Syria between 2011 and 2024, while Assad was president, Russia was Syria's main ally and military backer.

Assad was overthrown in December 2024, and now lives in exile in Moscow. Current Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa led an alliance of Islamist rebel groups that fought against government forces during the war.

Assad's ouster in 2024 dealt a major blow to Moscow's influence in the region.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been trying to build ties with Syria's new leadership to protect the future of the only two official Russian military bases located outside the former Soviet Union.

Al-Sharaa has met with Putin in Moscow twice since coming to power in January 2025.

During his last trip, Putin said, "much has been accomplished in terms of restoring our interstate relations."

The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Denmark: Several wounded in suspected gang shooting
entries.summary: Police said they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

Police said they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

Three people were wounded on Sunday in a shooting in Denmark.

They do not face life-threatening injuries, the police said.

Police said in a statement they believed that the incident was linked to a "settling of scores" within criminal networks.

"At this time, we cannot provide further information about their condition. The police presumption is that this is a settling of scores within the criminal milieu," the statement read.

Officers had been called to multiple locations in Holbaek, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) west of the capital, Copenhagen.

The incident was reported to police around 3:45 p.m. local time (1345 UTC).

Before the shots were fired, a fight broke out within a larger group in a residential estate, police said

Police said that the perpetrators were seen leaving the scene in a white car, according to preliminary information.

entries.title: Germany news: Berlin to step up drone security research
entries.summary: Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Meanwhile, the transport minister said he wants Deutsche Bahn bonuses tied to punctuality targets.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Berlin to step up drone security research

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 9, 2026

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Meanwhile, the transport minister said he wants Deutsche Bahn bonuses tied to punctuality targets.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that were hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 8-9, 2026:

  • Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says Germany is to expand drone security research
  • Algeria says it has taken charge of a German citizen kidnapped in Niger some two weeks ago
  • Low water levels in the Rhine and other rivers are posing a growing risk for Germany, an expert says
  • Protesters in eastern Germany have called for new elections, while demonstrators in Berlin have demanded a ban on far-right parties



Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section The Left could work with CDU to keep far-right AFD out of power

The Left could work with CDU to keep far-right AFD out of power

The co-leader of Die Linke ("The Left") on Sunday said the socialist party would do anything in its power to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) out of office.

Luigi Pantisano's remarks on public broadcaster ZDF come with less than a month to go before elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD is polling at over 40% and is poised to win an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Were the AfD to win in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it would mark Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

To prevent that scenario, Pantisano said he would consider supporting the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, despite Pantisano recently accusing the CDU of implementing "fascist politics."

"We, The Left, have shown in recent years that we take responsibility for this country," Pantisano told ZDF.

If the AfD falls short of an absolute majority, the CDU's incumbent state Premier Sven Schulze would likely have to form a coalition government with The Left.

The AfD has never been in government at either state or federal level, as all other established parties refuse to work with it, under a policy known as the "firewall."

Skip next section Transport minister wants Deutsch Bahn bonuses tied to punctuality targets

Transport minister wants Deutsch Bahn bonuses tied to punctuality targets

Germany's new transport minister, Steffen Bilger of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), said on Sunday that he planned to step up pressure on notoriously delayed railway operator Deutsche Bahn.

He told the mass-market Bild newspaper that bonus payments for Bahn managers would be impacted if government-set punctuality targets are not met.

"There will be a concrete impact on the bonus payments of rail managers if the targets set by the federal government are not met," Bilger said. "I think rail customers and taxpayers have a right to have success genuinely measured."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government is preparing a new financing agreement for the state-owned company that is to tie funding to specific targets.

Bilger took his ministerial post after Merz reshuffled his Cabinet last month, a move sparked by the resignation of senior conservative lawmaker Jens Spahn over a surrogacy scandal.

Deutsche Bahn is mired in a major structural crisis around delays and cancellations. In 2025, only 60% arrived on time or experienced delays of under six minutes, not including trains that were canceled or ended their journeys prematurely.

The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who are junior coalition partners in Merz's government, expressed support for the planned measure.

"I expressly welcome the fact that Transport Minister Bilger wants to link the bonus payments of rail managers to punctuality," the SPD's Isabel Cademartori told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"People expect the railway to become more reliable," she said. "As politicians, we are providing record investments in infrastructure and expect this to be reflected in punctuality."

Skip next section Nudist cyclists ride through Berlin for World Naked Bike Ride

Nudist cyclists ride through Berlin for World Naked Bike Ride

The German capital's first World Naked Bike Ride began in Berlin on Sunday.

Hundreds of people participated in the event, cycling either naked or partially naked through the streets of Berlin.

Organizers said that participants can join "dressed or undressed in whatever way they themselves feel most comfortable."

They said the event was to embody the idea that "naked we are all equal" and the German nudism movement, historically known as Freikörperkultur (meaning "free body culture" in Germany) or by the acronym FKK.

Organizers said they aimed to send a message of "tolerance and self-acceptance, closeness to nature and protection of the environment and for inclusion and diversity."

The German capital was experiencing hot weather of around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).

The event started in Mauerpark in eastern Berlin and proceeded to the government district.

Organizers said the route was to follow the Berlin Wall Trail to the Schönefeld neighborhood in the southeast of the Berlin metropolitan area. The suburb contains Berlin Brandenburg Airport.

Skip next section Berlin police investigating shooting incidents amid rise in gun crime

Berlin police investigating shooting incidents amid rise in gun crime

Berlin police are looking into two incidents in which shots were fired, as shooting incidents in the German capital seem on the rise.

In one incident early on Sunday, shots were fired at a hairdressing salon in the Marzahn-Hellersdorf district in the city's northeast, while a gunshot hole was also found at a nearby nightclub, a police spokeswoman said.

She said no one was injured.

That was, however, not the case with another shooting incident in Kreuzberg on Friday evening.

There, a 22-year-old man was shot and injured by an assailant, who fled the scene.

Homicide squad officers are investigating possible links to previous shooting incidents in the area.

Last year, Berlin police set up the Ferrum specialist unit to investigate gun crime.

Skip next section German national kidnapped in Niger freed — Algeria

German national kidnapped in Niger freed — Algeria

Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military. 

The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency.

He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date."

No details were provided on how the German national was freed.

A spokesperson for the German Foreign Ministry told DW it was aware of the case, but added that the government "does not comment on cases involving the abduction of German citizens abroad."

Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup, has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups.

Skip next section Trucks underway in several states as Sunday motorway ban lifted

Trucks underway in several states as Sunday motorway ban lifted

Several states have lifted a rule banning most trucks from using motorways on Sundays and public holidays in view of the low river water levels currently hampering cargo vessels.

The DPA news agency reported that a number of trucks have already been sighted on motorways in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW).

The NRW transport minister, Oliver Krischer, said that "this exceptional regulation allows us to ensure that delivery chains are maintained and supply shortages are avoided."

Industrial associations have welcomed the lifting of the truck ban.

But one of Germany's main unions, Verdi, has criticized the move.

"This measure comes at the cost of employees in the transport and logistics branch and calls into question the legal protection of Sundays and public holidays as days of rest and recreation," said Uwe Köpke, who heads the union's postal services, freight forwarding and logistics department.

Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are so far the only other states to have lifted the ban as one of the measures announced by Transport Minister Steffen Bilger last week to mitigate the economic effect of the cargo shipping shortfalls.

In NRW and Lower Saxony, the suspension of the ban is to run initially until August 31, and in Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland until September 30 at the latest.

In NRW, all trucks will also be able to use the motorways on Saturdays during the day in the current summer holidays as an exemption to an existing regulation.

Skip next section Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half of 2026

Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half of 2026

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year from January through June. German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises the trade deficit to about €55 billion ($63.6 billion) from €40 billion for the same period in 2025.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

Skip next section Rheinmetall's Papperger says he's not 'chickening out' amid threats

Rheinmetall's Papperger says he's not 'chickening out' amid threats

The CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, has said he will not be intimidated despite the many threats that have been made to his safety.

"These jobs must be done, and anyone that can't take the pressure doesn't belong in this job," he told the DPA news agency, saying "chickening out" was no option in his field.

Pappberger, 63, who is believed to be a possible target of Russian murder plots, is under constant police protection at a level similar to that given to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Rheinmetall is supplying large quantities of weapons to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, potentially putting the company in Moscow's crosshairs.  

Germany's domestic intelligence services recently called on employees in the defense sector to be very vigilant amid the threat of espionage and sabotage by Russian state agencies.

Skip next section Dobrindt announces stepped-up drone security research amid 'arms race'

Dobrindt announces stepped-up drone security research amid 'arms race'

Germany is establishing a new drone security research facility as it seeks to counter a growing threat from UAVs that are possibly under foreign control, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has told Sunday's edition of the Bild tabloid.

"The arms race in drone technology requires dedicated research units to keep pace," he said.

He said the new center, to be established on August 18 at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, would develop and test technologies to protect against drones.

His remarks come after a number of incidents involving drones in the past week raised security concerns.

You can read more on Dobrindt's statements on security here.

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

The DW newsroom in Bonn says a warm guten Morgen to its readers as we resume our coverage of all things German on Sunday.

Concerns about national security amid a myriad of threats are featuring largely in today's headlines, with, for example, the interior minister warning of hybrid warfare after several drone incidents.

Some of those threats even target particular people, as the CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, is experiencing.

And nature itself is also posing a security challenge, with the lack of water in the Rhine and other rivers having a widening impact on the economy and beyond.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage as the clock is about to strike midnight here in Bonn. Join us again on Sunday, when we will update this blog with the latest news from Germany.

Skip next section WATCH: CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power

WATCH: CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power

Sven Schulze, state premier and the CDU's candidate in the upcoming regional election in Saxony-Anhalt has slammed the AfD for its xenophobia, and underscored his state's reliance on exports and foreign workers.

Skip next section WATCH: Why low Rhine water levels are a growing risk for Germany

WATCH: Why low Rhine water levels are a growing risk for Germany

Germany's most important river is running low unusually early in the year.

Ships are still moving on the Rhine, but falling water levels are forcing many to carry lighter loads. Professor Kerstin Stahl, a hydrologist at the University of Freiburg, explains what is driving the drought and why the consequences reach far beyond shipping.

Skip next section Thousands call for Merz resignation, new elections at protest in eastern Germany

Thousands call for Merz resignation, new elections at protest in eastern Germany

Some 10,000 people protested in the eastern German city of Plauen to call for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's resignation and for new elections to be held immediately.

While the "Unity for Germany" protest was officially independent of political parties, a local pro-democracy group warned that some of the rally's organizers are right-wing extremists.

"The event is being promoted by relevant far-right channels; on Facebook, the comments on the demonstration contain hateful remarks, and the calls to action spread antisemitic and ethno-nationalist narratives," the Alliance for Democracy, Tolerance and Civil Courage said.

Apart from the government's resignation and new elections, the protesters' 11 demands also include:

  • The immediate deportation of 'all convicted, criminal and illegal migrants'

  • Lower energy prices

  • A

    cheaper nationwide monthly travel pass, for €29 ($33.50)

  • Reform to public service broadcasting

  • Scrapping the carbon dioxide tax

  • Introducing a direct democracy model like in Switzerland

  • Reducing bureaucracy

The protesters also chanted "We are the people," the slogan that was used at pro-democracy rallies during the peaceful revolution of 1989 in East Germany that preceded the end of the former German Democratic Republic.

Many German national flags, as well as banners of the historical Kingdom of Saxony — often used by the far-right Free Saxons party — were seen at the rally, as were blue peace flags with white doves, the German news agency dpa reported.

Skip next section Demonstrations in Germany call for ban on far-right parties

Demonstrations in Germany call for ban on far-right parties

Around 800 people demonstrated in Berlin, calling for the Federal Constitutional Court to review political parties suspected of right-wing extremism.

Eleven such demonstrations were planned across Germany on Saturday. The "Prüf," which translates to "check" or "examine," initiative, founded by activist Nico Semsrott, is behind the rallies.

Citing a legal opinion published in late June by the Society for Civil Rights that declared the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party unconstitutional, speakers called for a corresponding review by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Many of the demonstrators' posters bore the slogan, "Examine today — protect tomorrow."

However, the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, or the federal government must file a motion to ban the party in order to initiate such a review.

In early May 2025, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the AfD as a "confirmed far-right extremist movement," but suspended the designation after a legal challenge.

In February, a Cologne court said the agency can’t use the designation while the court evaluates the party’s lawsuit.

The AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

entries.title: Canada: British Columbia wildfires burning out of control
entries.summary: Wildfires have grown in number and intensity across British Columbia, where a state of emergency has been declared. Evacuations are underway, but firefighters say almost half of BC's 102 fires are out of control.
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

Wildfires have grown in number and intensity across British Columbia, where a state of emergency has been declared. Evacuations are underway, but firefighters say almost half of BC's 102 fires are out of control.

Wildfires raging in the western Canadian province of British Columbia gained momentum, growing significantly in both scale and intensity in a situation already declared a state of emergency on Saturday by British Columbia Minister of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness Kelly Greene.

By Sunday morning, the BC Wildfire Service reported 102 active blazes in the province (up from 70 on Saturday), nearly half of them out of control.

"Over the last 24 hours, extreme fire behavior was seen in southern BC due to the continuous hot and dry conditions," the service said, adding that response efforts were being hampered by "elevated fire behavior coupled with severely poor visibility."

The Bald Range fire — which exploded Saturday and enveloped the 12,000-resident Summerland area — had consumed nearly 10,341 hectares (25,552 acres) of land by early Sunday.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Sunday that it was "investigating to confirm" a possible fatality.

Officials have yet to provide casualty or damage figures, nor have they published a list of missing persons.

British Columbia Premier David Eby, who warned of the dangerous and unpredictable nature of the blaze on Saturday, said, "air evacuations are underway for people who remain isolated behind the fire perimeter."

"To everyone affected, you are not facing this alone," said Eby in a statement, "the entire province is with you."

Canadian media reported the airlifting of more than 50 people from the community of Faulder.

In all, more than 20,000 people have been forced to evacuate the area.

On Saturday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney took to X to thank firefighters and first responders for "working tirelessly to keep people safe."

Carney also pledged solidarity, writing: "The federal government stands ready to help and support the government of British Columbia in these efforts. I'm keeping everyone forced from their homes in my thoughts and hoping they can return safely soon."

entries.title: Divers in Italy find ancient Roman shipwreck, amphorae off coast of Sicily believed to be 2,100 years old
entries.summary: The wreck is believed to be more than 2,000 years old. Italy's culture minister says it is "one of the most important underwater archaeological" finds in years.
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

The wreck is believed to be more than 2,000 years old. Italy's culture minister says it is "one of the most important underwater archaeological" finds in years.

Divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, Italian police said.

The shipwreck is believed to be 2,100 years old.

The wreck had been found approximately three nautical miles off the coast of Mazaro del Vallo in western Sicily at a depth of 46 meters (150 feet), police said  in a statement.

The cultural protection arm of the Italian police (Carabinieri) called it a "significant underwater archaeological site." It added that initial surveys had "identified a Roman shipwreck presumably dating to between the 2nd and 1st centuries BC."

Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli has called the find "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years."

The site also contains "hundreds" of amphorae, which would likely have been used to transport wine.

How was the ancient Roman shipwreck discovered?

The shipwreck was found after a tip-off from local fishermen. Calling it the "most incredible discovery of my life," Giacomo De Mola described on Instagram how he had stumbled upon the ancient wreck, which he said at first looked like "a simple rock."

"Visibility isn't great. I see a large dark mass and think, 'Just another big rock…' I get even closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock. Beneath me lay an immense expanse of amphorae — hundreds of amphorae that have lain on the seafloor for over 2,000 years. A Roman ship slumbering in the silence of the Mediterranean," De Mola said.

In the post, the diver also included footage of the find.

Local media report that the ship is 21 meters long and 6 meters wide, and that it was mainly transporting Dressel 1A amphorae, tall cylindrical ceramic jars that were mainly used to carry wine.

De Mola said Lamboglia 2 amphorae, presumably from North Africa, as well as a Neo-Punic amphora, were also found.

"An extraordinary testament to the Mediterranean trade routes of over 2,000 years ago," the diver said.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Middle East: Netanyahu says Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan
entries.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced Israel's rejection of US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza.
entries.content:
Iran

Middle East: Netanyahu says Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 9, 2026

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced Israel's rejection of US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, PM Netanyahu says

  • Houthi rebels claim attack on Saudi oil facility

  • The Revolutionary Guard says Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz once the US 'corrects its behavior' and accepts Iran's conditions
  • They include never threatening Iran again, lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets
  • The Guards also say the strategic waterway's reopening does not depend on how talks with Oman develop
  • Iran says the talks are nearing their 'final' stages, with Oman calling the discussions 'positive'
  • The UAE says Iran targeted tanker transiting in Hormuz

This blog is closed. It covered the latest developments on the conflict in the Middle East on Saturday, August 8, and Sunday, August 9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section US 'low-keying it' with Iran, Trump tells reporter

US 'low-keying it' with Iran, Trump tells reporter

President Donald Trump suggested in a phone call with the Axios media outlet that the US was willing to wait for a peace agreement with Iran.

"We are low-keying it," he said, according to Axios. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."

Trump expressed his optimism that a satisfactory conclusion would eventually be reached.

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he said of the war.

 

Skip next section Pentagon urges US defense sector to ramp up production, delivery of weapons: reports

Pentagon urges US defense sector to ramp up production, delivery of weapons: reports

The Pentagon has urged the US defense industry to accelerate weapons production and delivery, several US media outlets reported on Sunday.

A memo from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, written on Wednesday, gave the defense industry three weeks to table plans for faster delivery times and/or increased production, The Washington Post and broadcaster CNN reported.

There have been reports of the US military's dwindling weapons stocks due to the Iran war. US President Donald Trump has sought to downplay the situation.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who was appointed by Trump at the start of his second term in January last year, has pushed the Pentagon to increase the speed, effectiveness and capacity of the US defense industry, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

"Working directly with industry leaders to accelerate production is not new," Parnell said.

At the end of July, the US had fewer than 830 Patriot defense missiles, compared to over 2,300 at the start of the war with Iran five months ago, according to estimates by the Washington-based Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

CSIS also estimates that the US had 452 THAAD interceptor missiles before the war, a figure that had fallen to as few as 278 missiles at the end of July, the think tank said.

At a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing last month, Hegseth said the war had so far cost $37.5 billion (around €32.6 billion).

During that hearing, Hegseth, whose department has been renamed the Department of War , was grilled about his request for a $1.5 trillion defense budget, which included nearly $70 billion for the war with Iran.

The US already spends around $1 trillion per year on defense, or around $2.7 billion per day.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Washington spends more on defense than China, Russia, Germany, India, the UK, Ukraine and Saudi Arabia — the next seven largest defense spenders — combined.

Skip next section WATCH: Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank

WATCH: Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank

The Israeli military has intensified its raids in the occupied West Bank. Meanwhile, Israeli settler violence continues almost unchecked, forcing Palestinians to form volunteer groups to protect their villages.   

Skip next section Syria says it reached deal with Russia on future of Tartous and Hmeimim bases

Syria says it reached deal with Russia on future of Tartous and Hmeimim bases

Following 18 months of negotiations, Syria and Russia reached a memorandum of understanding to settle the future of Russian bases at Tartous and Hmeimim, the Syrian Foreign Ministry announced.

According to the ministry's statement, cited by the official SANA news agency, the Syrian state will take over management of civilian facilities, including the Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at the Tartous port. This will allow the facilities to be gradually integrated into the country's civilian administration.

Meanwhile, military facilities will be repurposed as joint training and qualification centers under new arrangements that preserve the interests of both sides. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, the ministry said.

The Hmeimim airbase and the Tartus naval base are Russia's only two official military bases outside of the former Soviet Union.

During the 13-year civil war in Syria, Russia was a key ally of former Syrian leader Bashar Assad, providing vital military support that helped keep Assad's forces in power.

Skip next section Hamas says US must pressure Netanyahu to accept Gaza deal — AFP

Hamas says US must pressure Netanyahu to accept Gaza deal — AFP

After Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the US-backed Gaza peace plan, a Hamas official told the AFP news agency that the United States must pressure Israel to accept the next phase of the plan.

"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," AFP cited Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim as saying.

Earlier, Hamas said it had agreed to the plan to spare the people of Gaza from a possible resumption of war. However, the militant group added that the deal's implementation would depend on Israel first meeting its commitments, including withdrawal from the Gaza Strip.

Skip next section Iran vows to release footage of Supreme Leader

Iran vows to release footage of Supreme Leader

Mizan, the Iranian judiciary's news outlet, reported that a Basij Organization deputy head promised to release footage of the Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei at a later time.

Footage of Khamenei "among the people and out in streets, as well ‌in meetings ⁠with ⁠the commanders of armed forces" will be ​released in the future, Qasem Qoraishi reportedly said.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who was appointed Supreme Leader in March, has not been seen in public since his appointment.

According to senior Iranian sources, he suffered facial disfigurement and other injuries in the strike that killed his father on February 28, the first day of US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran.

Skip next section Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, Netanyahu says

Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, Netanyahu says

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that Israel has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza.

The prime minister stressed that the Israeli military will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document. The IDF (Israel's military, known as the Israel Defense Forces) will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting.

Last month, Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached a "historic" agreement with Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups in the Gaza Strip to disarm.

Israel designates Hamas as a terrorist group, alongside several other countries including the United States and Germany.

Skip next section Houthis attack government-controlled port of Mocha in Yemen

Houthis attack government-controlled port of Mocha in Yemen

A Yemeni government official said the Houthis attacked the crucial Red Sea port of Mocha.

Fayed al-Noman, the assistant undersecretary of the Information Ministry, said the Houthis launched missiles and drones at Mocha.

At least seven people were killed and 20 others injured in an attack, a Yemeni government military source told dpa. According to the source, the fatalities included three civilians and four military personnel who were present at the port.

Meanwhile, a medical source told AFP that there had been 11 casualties and over 30 injuries.

Mocha is one of the main ports under the control of Yemen's internationally recognized government backed by Saudi Arabia.

It was renovated in recent years to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held ports in Hodeida.

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attack. According to Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree, the movement’s forces carried out a “large-scale and precise” operation targeting Saudi enemy troops and weapons depots in the Mocha area.

Earlier on Sunday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for attacking the Saudi Aramco oil facility in Jizan that caused a fire.

Skip next section Iran: Talks with US won't take place while interim deal is breached

Iran: Talks with US won't take place while interim deal is breached

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no negotiations between Iran and the United States, only an exchange of messages through intermediaries.

In remarks published by the Mehr news agency and cited by Reuters, Araghchi also said Tehran would not begin negotiations as long as Washington continued to breach the interim deal signed in June.

He reiterated Iran's stance that an agreement between Tehran and Muscat on the Strait of Hormuz was in the "final stages," though it would not reopen the strategic waterway.

Araghchi said the agreement would establish new shipping lanes to be used once the US fulfills its conditions and reopens the Strait of Hormuz to traffic.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guards also said they would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States accepts all of Tehran's demands.

"Our current strategy is to maintain this strait until the enemy accepts all our conditions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state TV, according to AFP.

He added that "the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway."

Skip next section Houthis say they hit refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast

Houthis say they hit refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility on Sunday for a strike on an oil facility along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted an Aramco refinery in the city of Jazan with a drone.

He added the attack was in response to Saudi drones that had breached Yemen’s airspace over the provinces of Hajjah and Saada.

Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery, adding that there were no casualties.

The ministry said the fire had been extinguished, but did not describe its cause. Aramco is Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

Good morning! We are reopening our blog after a nighttime break.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis on the situation in the Middle East.

Skip next section What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

Earlier, DW reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said talks with the United States on reopening the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington's "compensating" Iran for the US "violation" of a June memorandum of understanding that the two nations had signed.

Aragchi and the IRGC had also pointed to "other conditions" that would need to be met.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council said the country would not lift its blockade of Hormuz until the United States "corrects its behavior."

In a statement by the council's secretary and Revolutionary Guard Commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr that was published on Iran's state broadcaster, said the United States must:

  • Never threaten Iran again
  • Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip
  • Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area
  • Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets 

The US has yet to respond.

Skip next section WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

Iran says it is in the final stages of reaching an agreement with Oman on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Reports suggest that the deal would give Tehran oversight of vessels entering the Persian Gulf. Oman would manage outbound traffic.

If finalized, the arrangement could mark a significant shift in regional influence and raise questions about freedom of navigation, security and the balance of power in the Gulf.

DW spoke to analyst Megan Sutcliffe and former US diplomat Alan Eyre, who helped negotiate the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, about what this could mean for the region and beyond.

Skip next section Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

On Friday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled a new security alliance that bears strong similarities to NATO's principles of collective defense.

The three regional powers — who are also strategic allies of the United States — have signed a defense pact that is "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The deal is widely viewed as the three Sunni-majority nations' way of defending themselves against the rising threat from an increasingly hostile Iran, where Shiite Islam is the state religion.

The agreement could also be seen as a sign of shifting power dynamics in the region, as well as a way to hedge against an unreliable US, amid uncertainty over its long-term commitment to its role in enforcing security in the Gulf.

DW's Brent Goff spoke to experts Dania Thafer and Kamran Bokhari to learn more about what the new agreement means for the region and the US-Iran conflict.

Skip next section Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman's Foreign Ministry on Saturday said talks with Iran about the future of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz were "proceeding in a positive and constructive atmosphere."

But Muscat warned against "repeated attacks" on cargo ships, which it said could jeopardize the negotiations, although it stopped short of explicitly naming Iran.

Tehran has been targeting ships that it claims have ties to the United States or that fail to comply with its orders.

Earlier on Saturday, Iran said talks over a deal with Oman were "approaching the final stages."

entries.title: Ukraine and Russia exchange attacks as Kyiv buys new ATACMS
entries.summary: Overnight drone and missile attacks killed several and injured dozens more in both Ukraine and Russia. As Kyiv seeks to defend itself it has now reportedly finalized a deal to buy US missile systems from Turkey.
entries.content:
Europe

Ukraine and Russia exchange attacks as Kyiv buys new ATACMS

August 9, 2026

Overnight drone and missile attacks killed several and injured dozens more in both Ukraine and Russia. As Kyiv seeks to defend itself it has now reportedly finalized a deal to buy US missile systems from Turkey.

Overnight drone and missile attacks have killed several people and injured dozens more according to various local authorities in Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Russian city of Belgorod, near the Ukrainian border, at least five people were killed and 25 injured.

Belgorod's acting governor said that several apartment blocks had been hit overnight and images posted to social media showed several fires.

Belgorod is a key logistics hub for Russian offensives in Kharkiv and the Donbass.

Russian authorities, who said more than 150 Ukrainian drones had been downed by their forces overnight, also reported attacks on the Black Sea ports of Novorossiysk and Gelendzhik.

Novorossiysk is home to key Russian oil export facilities.

'Russia continuing its war on global food security' says Zelenskyy

Russian attacks targeted oil refineries in the Sumy region as well as the port city of Odesa, where President Voldymyr Zelenskyy said at least eight people had been injured.

The Odesa strikes targeted oil facilities in the southern port.

Odesa is also one of Ukraine's most important agricultural export hubs.

Zelenskyy said that with Sunday's attack, "Russia is continuing its war on global food security."

Two people were also killed and at least 21 injured in a Russian attack on Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov.

Across the border, Russia claimed its forces had taken control of two villages in eastern Donetsk, though the claim could not be independently verified.

Kyiv arming itself against 4-year Russia invasion

As Russia's war on Ukraine drags on toward the five-year mark, Kyiv is again short on defensive weapons.

Kyiv has desperately sought to acquire more medium and long-range weapons systems from the US with mixed results.

Now, Ukraine is turning to Turkey for help as the US reportedly depletes its own stockpiles with its still unresolved war in Iran.

On Sunday, Ukraine's military news outlet Militarnyi reported that it would be purchasing 70 ATACMS and 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems from Turkey in an order that will also include more than 2,500 227mm rockets with cluster-munitions payloads.

The US, which has 30 days to approve the sale, estimates its total value at $283 million (€245 million).

The ATACMS in question are of an older design, with a range limited to 165 kilometers (102.5 miles).

Edited by: Rana Taha
